items.title: Psychological pathways to sustainable employee performance: the roles of digital leadership, psychological empowerment, work engagement, and organizational trust
items.abstract: The digital transformation of organizations has intensified interest in the psychological factors associated with employees’ ability to sustain effective performance over time. However, limited research has examined the relationships between digital leadership, psychological empowerment, organizational trust, work engagement, and sustainable employee performance within an integrated framework. Drawing on Social Exchange Theory and the Job Demands–Resources model, this study examines these relationships in digitally transforming organizations in China. Survey data were collected from 550 employees and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The results supported all seven hypotheses. Digital leadership was positively associated with psychological empowerment and organizational trust, while psychological empowerment and organizational trust were positively associated with work engagement. Work engagement was also positively associated with sustainable employee performance. The mediation analyses indicated significant indirect relationships between digital leadership and sustainable employee performance through work engagement and through the sequential pathway involving psychological empowerment and work engagement. These findings highlight the relevance of psychological resources and motivational states in understanding sustainable employee performance in digitally transforming workplaces. The study contributes to research on digital leadership by integrating empowerment, trust, and engagement within a framework grounded in Social Exchange Theory and the Job Demands–Resources model. For practitioners, the findings suggest that leadership practices supporting employee autonomy, trust, and engagement may be relevant to maintaining effective performance over time. Given the cross-sectional design, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of associations rather than causal effects.

items.title: Psychological resilience, emotional regulation, and performance pressure in Formula One: A documentary thematic analysis of public driver narratives
items.abstract: Formula One (F1) represents one of the most psychologically demanding environments in elite sport, requiring athletes to perform under conditions of extreme cognitive workload, physiological strain, public scrutiny, and competitive uncertainty. Despite growing recognition of athlete mental health and well-being, limited research has explored how Formula One drivers themselves construct and interpret experiences of performance pressure, emotional regulation, resilience, and identity across their careers. This study employed a documentary, media-based Reflexive Thematic Analysis, informed by a critical realist epistemology, to examine how elite Formula One drivers publicly construct experiences of performance pressure, emotional regulation, resilience, and identity. Data were drawn from publicly available press conference transcripts, podcasts, and published interviews involving 14 current and former Formula One drivers. Analysis was guided by contemporary frameworks of psychological resilience, athletic identity, and transactional stress appraisal. Four interrelated themes were generated: (1) The Dualism of Perfectionism and Self-Blame, (2) Preternatural Equanimity and Functional Appraisal, (3) Narrative Identity and Career Reconstruction, (4) The Interplay of Cognitive Control, Adversity, and Mental Toughness. Findings suggest that, as publicly narrated, resilience in Formula One is not presented as a fixed personality trait but as a dynamic process shaped by cognitive appraisal, emotional regulation, social support, and identity development. These findings provide an account of how drivers construct and communicate psychological adaptation for public audiences, rather than direct evidence of their underlying psychological states. The study contributes to the emerging literature on athlete mental health by providing insight into how psychological adaptation is publicly represented and communicated within one of the world's most demanding sporting contexts. Implications for sport psychology practice, athlete welfare, and integrated mental health support systems in elite motorsport are discussed.

items.title: Psychotherapy 2035: Generative Ai Scenarios Psychotherapy 2035: A Technology Assessment Review of Generative AI Scenarios for Mental Health Care
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is entering psychotherapy faster than evidence, professional norms and regulation can follow, the configuration described by the Collingridge dilemma. This technology assessment review combines a narrative synthesis of PubMed and web searches (9 October 2026) with explorative scenario construction along two axes, locus of delivery and governance regime. Efficacy effects are small, short-lived and heterogeneous; blended and certified formats are better supported than stand-alone chatbots. Documented harms, including inadequate crisis responses, dependence and distress after model updates, concentrate outside clinical settings, and regulation is fragmented. Four scenarios result for 2035: augmented clinician, stepped hybrid care, consumer-companion market and regulated digital therapeutics. They will probably coexist. Governance should prioritize measures that are robust across scenarios (outcome and incident registries, crisis-escalation standards, continuity duties, protected human roles) and monitor early signposts.

items.title: Recursive Collective Intelligence: Emergence on an Equal-Budget Ladder in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly work as teams of agents, and a team is expected to solve problems beyond the reach of any single member. Most evaluations credit a team for outperforming a single agent, without accounting for the additional computation: a team may consume many times the tokens of one agent, and a plain vote over independent answers already explains most of the reported gain. Two questions therefore remain open: When does interaction itself make a group smarter, and can a group improve its next generation by learning from its own work? We answer both with the equal-budget ladder, which grades a group against independent agents at three levels: outperforming a single agent, a compute-matched majority vote, and compute-matched pass@n. On this ladder we define Recursive Collective Intelligence (RCI) as a group whose own output, without a teacher or external labels, makes its next generation smarter at equal cost. Three findings follow. First, interaction improves collective intelligence when it moves information across agents: forwarding split facts lifts groups above pass@n at three model scales, by about a third at 27B. Second, organization emerges spontaneously: identical 27B agents form hubs and improve accuracy by 18 percentage points; encoding their organization in a prompt enables them to reach level 3 at less than half the token budget in a descriptive comparison. Third, groups recursively improve themselves: Two label-free generations progressively climb the ladder, the second 9B generation surpassing both pass@$n$ and a control trained on base-model turns; on PlanBench, HiddenBench and Hanabi, each generation outperforms its predecessor on unseen problems for four to six generations. A group therefore outperforms its members when it forwards useful information more efficiently than it spends tokens on coordination, and learns to do so from its own work.

items.title: Recursive entanglement drift: Arbitration shift as a candidate mechanism of relational-epistemic risk in human–AI interaction
items.abstract: Recent work on harmful human–AI interaction has moved from anecdotal reports towards measurement, including research showing how AI sycophancy can produce erroneous beliefs even in idealized rational users. Much of this work focuses on what users believe and what models reinforce, while less is known about how users settle conflicts when an AI-mediated interpretation and an outside source disagree. This paper proposes Recursive Entanglement Drift (RED), a longitudinal framework for relational-epistemic risk in human–AI interaction that describes how recursive exchanges may form a sealed dyad, where outside correction remains present but loses influence. AI outputs can shape subsequent user inputs, which then shape later AI responses. RED's proposed core mechanism is arbitration shift, a change over time toward the AI-mediated frame in epistemic arbitration, the process by which users resolve conflicts between previously AI-mediated commitments and sources outside the human–AI dyad. Source-conflict episodes can document how individual disagreements resolve, while arbitration shift is inferred across episodes within the same user. The paper includes a codebook designed to complement existing transcript-coding systems. Its potential explanatory value beyond trust, dependence, and general belief-revision tendencies remains to be empirically tested. Users may rely heavily on AI while outside sources still influence how conflicts resolve, and the shift may appear with limited emotional or functional reliance on AI. Arbitration shift is predicted to precede stable resistance to correction. If supported, it may provide an early marker of risk not defined by belief content or accuracy; if unsupported, the construct should be revised or rejected.

items.title: Risk of Bias Assessment Tools for Evidence Synthesis: Evolution, Comparison, and Future Directions in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: A risk-of-bias assessment judges whether flaws in the design, conduct, or analysis of a study could have distorted its effect estimate. Appraisal tools for this task have multiplied, and large language models, a form of artificial intelligence, are now being tested as assessors. This narrative review covers 59 tools for appraising the risk of bias or methodological quality of studies (1981–2026) identified from earlier overviews or organizational resources supplemented by PubMed searches for new tools. This review traces over time three overlapping lines of development: summed scores, structured checklists, and domain-based tools to assess studies against an ideal trial. It compares the seven tools currently recommended for the main study designs, examines their use in traditional Chinese medicine and other complex interventions, and appraises published evidence on assessments using large language models. Domain-based tools pose a clearer causal question than earlier tools but are harder to apply consistently. In reliability studies, chance-corrected agreement between independent assessors was low for the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2; Fleiss' κ 0.16, 95% confidence interval 0.08–0.24) and for the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions tool (ROBINS-I; κ 0.06, 95% confidence interval 0.001–0.12). Surveys of reviews show that tools are often poorly chosen and their results unused. Moreover, in traditional Chinese medicine trials, sham acupuncture is not physiologically inert, acupuncturists cannot be blinded, and syndrome-based tailoring is part of the intended intervention only when specified by the protocol; therefore, reviewers must check protocols and registrations. These features call for judgment when RoB 2 is applied, rather than an automatic high-risk rating. Finally, published evaluations of language models differ in terms of models, prompts, tools, samples, reference standards, and metrics; therefore, their results cannot be compared directly. Overall agreement with human judgments on RoB 2 was found to be low to moderate (κ 0.06 to 0.51), and the models are not yet suitable as stand-alone assessors. Here, we propose a conceptual human-in-the-loop workflow in which software retrieves and anchors evidence, trained reviewers make every judgment, and any use of artificial intelligence is fully reported. This approach requires prospective testing of accuracy, agreement, override rates, and total person-time. Priorities for tool development include application guidance for RoB 2 in traditional medicine trials, tested for consistency among assessors; a bias module for trials of artificial intelligence interventions; open benchmark datasets; and signaling questions at the design stage. items.title: SafeCalib: benchmarking security-critical refusal calibration in instruction-tuned language models
items.abstract: Instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as gatekeepers for security-sensitive and dual-use requests, yet most AI safety evaluations report refusal as a binary outcome. This leaves a deployment-critical question underexamined: whether a model separates harmful requests from legitimate security work reliably, and whether that separation survives adversarial framing. We introduce a refusal-evaluation framework comprising a two-sided, intensity-stratified error measure—Calibration-Adapted Expected Calibration Error (CA-ECE)—paired Overrefusal/Underrefusal Rate (ORR/URR) measurement, and Adversarial Calibration Shift (ACS), a statistic for how far underrefusal erodes as adversarial prompt framing intensifies. We state its scope explicitly: a refusal decision carries no confidence score, so CA-ECE is not a probability-calibration error but the fixed-weight average $$\tfrac{1}{2}(\bar{\textrm{URR}}+\bar{\textrm{ORR}})$$, whose neutral value 0.5 is shared by any policy that always refuses or never refuses. We instantiate the framework with SafeCalibBench, a 6,080-prompt benchmark covering malware generation, phishing, social engineering, network exploitation and chemical/biological misuse, with binary refusal labels, five adversarial intensity levels and legitimate-security-research hard negatives. Evaluating four instruction-tuned LLMs and three base counterparts on a stratified 2,000-prompt subsample, with intervals from a base-prompt-level cluster bootstrap, we find a consistent tradeoff: instruction tuning reduces direct underrefusal by 58.9 percentage points on average relative to base models but raises overrefusal by 20.0 points (mean ORR $$=24.6\%$$). Base-model CA-ECE (0.506–0.518) lies within 0.02 of the content-independent baseline of 0.5, so their low overrefusal reflects indiscriminate acceptance; instruction-tuned models reach 0.336–0.443. Continuation framing raises underrefusal by up to 37.7 points relative to direct prompts, and refusal behaviour differs significantly across security domains ($$p<0.01$$). All estimates carry a signed, asymmetric classifier bias that we characterise rather than assume away. SafeCalib reframes refusal evaluation from whether a model refused to how far its refusals separate harmful from legitimate use.

items.title: Seeing Through the Lens: Divergent Thinking and the Evaluation of Creative Product Designs
items.abstract: Evaluations of creative products reflect both product characteristics and evaluator attributes. It remains unclear whether the ability to generate original ideas shapes how people evaluate creative products made by others. In this preregistered study, 97 university students first completed the Gough Creative Personality Scale, the openness items of the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and a self-report item on cultural orientation. In random order, they then rated five iconic chair designs on the Creative Product Semantic Scale and completed an Alternative Uses Task with six everyday objects. items.title: Self regulated learning in vocational education: A bibliometric and systematic literature review of an emerging research field
items.abstract: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) is increasingly recognized as a crucial competency for navigating the complexities of vocational training; however, its structural evolution as a distinct research field remains fragmented. This study systematically maps the global research landscape of vocational SRL through a hybrid approach combining bibliometric analysis and a systematic literature review (SLR). Executed on a refined corpus of 43 Scopus-indexed articles published between 2003 and 2026, data visualization and performance analysis were performed using VOSviewer, the bibliometrix package in RStudio, and Microsoft Excel. The temporal analysis identified three developmental phases, highlighting an unprecedented publication surge from 2022 onwards, which peaked in 2025 with nine articles. Keyword co-occurrence mapping uncovered four robust thematic clusters: (1) SRL and Its Related Factors in Vocational Contexts; (2) Theoretical and Methodological Foundations; (3) Problem-Based and E-Learning Approaches; and (4) Motivation, Reflection, and Learning Strategies. Geographically, the Netherlands leads global productivity-anchored by Maastricht University and the Open University-with Vocations and Learning emerging as the flagship journal, while Asian countries such as Taiwan, China, Indonesia, and Malaysia show rapidly expanding contributions. Substantively, a systematic synthesis of 15 core articles-purposefully selected from 43 articles based on full-text accessibility and thematic richness-shows that metacognition (planning, monitoring, and reflection) plays a crucial role in supporting vocational autonomy, strongly underpinned by motivation and self-efficacy, while goal setting and behavioral regulation prove critical in work-based apprenticeship settings. These findings carry important theoretical implications, particularly highlighting the need for frameworks that accommodate competency-based training and experiential workplace learning. Practically, the results call for strengthened teacher training in SRL scaffolding, adaptive digital learning platforms, and closer institutional-industry collaboration. Ultimately, this review offers an initial reference for the field, urging future research to prioritize longitudinal designs, culturally validated measurement instruments, broader geographic representation, and the exploration of SRL's role in cultivating entrepreneurial competencies.

items.title: ShellBench: What Matters More for AI Agents, Models, or Harness for Everyday Tasks
items.abstract: The use of AI agents among the general public has been increasing exponentially throughout 2026, though it is often hard for users to determine which configuration is most effective for their personal use. To help provide clarity here we introduce ShellBench, 100 day-to-day tasks based on more than 10 million user requests, each set in a realistic workspace with messy files and competing data sources, and graded for both correctness and safety. We evaluate 12 models across 5 agent harnesses at 3 reasoning levels for a total of 53,100 rollouts, 20% of which are on tasks designated for public release. We find that model choice impacts performance more than harness choice, but the three leading models differ by only 1.1 percentage points. GPT-6.1 Sol passed 61.4% of attempts at about one-sixth of GPT-6 Astra's estimated token cost per attempt, while GPT-6 Astra led at 62.5%. We also found that harness choice had little effect on either performance or safety with all harnesses scoring between 42.9 (Claude Code) and 45.2 (OpenClaw) for pass@1.

items.title: Shifting confidence, not choices: Moral bias and social influence in human-LLM conversations
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in everyday decision-making, yet their influence on human moral judgment remains poorly understood. Prior research has largely tracked binary opinion reversal as the primary outcome, overlooking a more consequential pathway: modulation of the certainty with which moral positions are held, which can shape downstream behaviors and susceptibility to social influence. To test this, we conducted two experiments (N = 120 each) in which online samples of US adults ( M ag e = 38.6, SD = 10.4, 40.8% female) conversed with a morally framed LLM (utilitarian, deontological, or balanced) about autonomous vehicle moral dilemmas. Experiment 2 extended this to a two-stage social cascade in which downstream participants received either LLM- or human-generated summaries of prior human–LLM conversations. Results showed that binary moral decisions were highly stable. Confidence increased across all three bias conditions in both experiments, and confidence-weighted opinion strength shifted toward the LLM's framing. In the predominantly utilitarian sample, alignment was associated with confidence gains, whereas misalignment shifted opinion direction without reducing confidence. Experiment 2 used highly aligned summaries to model a high-risk cascade. Surprisingly, moral-bias effect sizes were descriptively smaller in Experiment 2 than in Experiment 1, although the between-experiment interaction was not significant. Deontological framing was descriptively more resilient, and AI-generated summaries produced a stronger deontological shift than human-generated summaries. In these experiments, LLM dialogue influenced confidence even when choices remained stable; whether this pattern generalizes to other models, moral dilemmas, and populations remains to be tested.

items.title: Short-Term Efficiency, Long-Term Cognitive Cost? A Systematic Literature Review of Large Language Model Use in Professional Work
items.abstract: Many professionals now use large language models (LLMs) at work, and experiments show that the tools make many tasksfaster and improve the immediate output. The worry is that these gains may cost workers some of the skill, judgement and self-knowledgethey would otherwise build or keep. We systematically reviewed empirical research on the cognitive and performance consequences ofLLM use among workers and professionals, published between January 2020 and November 2026. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines,we identified 1,559 records in OpenAlex and Europe PMC and five further studies through citation searching. After screening, 157 studiesremained. Two-thirds were published in 2026, and most come from software development, healthcare and general knowledge work.Randomised and field experiments consistently report short-term gains in speed, output and quality, typically largest for less experiencedworkers. These gains are task-dependent, and LLM-assisted professionals frequently fail to match the model working alone. Fewer than tenstudies measured unaided performance, memory or skill after LLM use. Those that did reported reduced recall of AI-assisted work,impaired skill formation and fragility when access was disrupted. Cross-sectional studies link reliance and confidence in AI with lowerself-reported critical thinking and professional self-efficacy, but self-reported capability loss did not track objective performance.Experience, task fit, mode of use, AI literacy and verification behaviour emerged as moderators. We conclude that the short-term efficiencygain is well supported, while the long-term cognitive cost remains plausible but largely untested in professional settings. We propose aframework and research agenda centred on longitudinal and withdrawal-based designs.

items.title: Single camera computer vision to estimate trunk angles during dynamic manual materials handling work
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine how video capture angle, computer vision platform, and movement pace influence trunk and shoulder angle estimates during manual materials handling (MMH) tasks relative to a multi-camera motion capture system. BACKGROUND: Posture assessment is important for evaluating musculoskeletal disorder (MSD) hazards during MMH work, yet limited guidance exists on how to optimally implement emerging computer vision technologies to inform posture assessment. METHODS: Forty participants performed three common MMH tasks. Video data from eight cameras positioned around the participant were processed using Theia3D to generate criterion trunk inclination and shoulder elevation angles. Individual camera views were also processed through four commercially available single-camera computer vision platforms. Mean absolute differences (MADs) between multi-camera and single-camera angle estimates were calculated. RESULTS: Camera viewing angle had a larger effect on MAD than computer vision platform. Recording lifting, palletizing, or pushing/pulling from directly in front of or behind the participant performed worst (e.g., MAD>20°), regardless of computer vision platform. However, the optimal camera viewing angle (e.g., perspective that limited MAD to ≈5°, or less) was dependent on the computer vision platform used. CONCLUSION/APPLICATION: Computer vision platforms produced consistent differences for all evaluated segments when the camera views captured MMH work from their optimal viewing angle. Users should avoid recording MMH work from anterior or posterior views.

items.title: Stakeholder Acceptance, Trust, and Implementation of AI in Oncology: Mixed Methods Systematic Review
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: AI is entering oncology workflows faster than evidence on stakeholder acceptance, trust, and sustained use. Existing syntheses rarely distinguish anticipated attitudes from actual use across oncology stakeholders. OBJECTIVE: The aim of the study is to synthesize primary empirical evidence on stakeholder acceptance, trust, and implementation of AI in oncology and examine variation by stakeholder group, clinical task, AI exposure, and implementation maturity. METHODS: We conducted a Joanna Briggs Institute-guided mixed methods systematic review with convergent integrated synthesis; the protocol was registered before formal eligibility screening. Eight databases were searched without date or language limits (August 6-9, 2026), yielding 46,206 records and 31,802 unique records. Title and abstract screening used 2 balanced primary allocations, joint bidirectional readjudication, and blinded verification of a stratified 10% (n=3182) sample. Full-text assessment, extraction, and critical appraisal were dual independent. Acceptance/Trust modes and F1-F8 coverage were independently coded across 309 studies and reconciled. Eight integrated findings were anchored to the nonadoption, abandonment, scale-up, spread, and sustainability framework; an emergent economic finding was reported separately. Adjusted stage models controlled for study design, publication format, and publication period; robustness analyses examined screening provenance and appraisal sensitivity. RESULTS: We included 309 primary empirical studies; 187 (60.5%) were published in 2025 or 2026. Exposure ranged from hypothetical opinion to real-world implementation (n=82 studies), but only 6 described routine use. Acceptance was empirically assessed in 267 studies and Trust in 127. Relative to anticipatory stage 1, Acceptance assessment was less frequent in evaluated-interaction stage 2 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.07, 95% CI 0.02-0.25; P<.001) and stages 3+4 (aOR 0.12, 95% CI 0.03-0.45; P=.001). Transparency/explainability coverage (F3) was lower in stages 3+4 (aOR 0.20, 95% CI 0.08-0.47; q<0.001). Workflow/interoperability coverage (F5) was higher and governance coverage (F7) lower in both later contrasts after false discovery rate correction. Trust declined descriptively across stages, but adjusted contrasts were nonsignificant. Eight integrated findings spanned clinical value, performance, transparency, oversight, workflow, readiness, governance, and implementation, plus an emergent stage 1 economic finding. The principal Acceptance, F3, F5, and F7 findings persisted in the 229-study original screening subset. CONCLUSIONS: In oncology, the AI evidence profile appears to differ from anticipated use to implementation. Acceptance was empirically assessed most often before deployment; later-stage studies more often examined workflow and less often examined transparency and governance. The challenge is whether favorable attitudes and early deployment translate into calibrated, governed, and sustained routine use. An interpretive stage-specific model identifies assessment priorities across exposure and implementation contexts, but is not a validated causal or predictive model. Later-stage evaluations should retain measurement of Acceptance, trust calibration, governance, durability, and workflow outcomes. items.title: Strategic leadership in AI-assisted banking decisions: a conceptual framework for critical evaluation and accountability
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly informs strategic banking decisions, yet the presence of human reviewers does not establish that critical evaluation influences organisational commitment. This article examines how strategic leadership can organise the assessment, challenge, and authorisation of AI-assisted strategic recommendations. Drawing on a targeted, non-exhaustive synthesis of research on strategic leadership, human–AI delegation, employee voice, accountability, and AI governance, it develops a conceptual framework centred on the strategic decision episode. The framework connects three processes: independent assessment, consequential challenge, and reasoned commitment. It distinguishes the expression of a material objection from the substantive response it receives and the incorporation of that response into the grounds for authorisation. Six propositions propose how model opacity, verification resources, sponsor control, prospective justification, and independent assessments supplied to approvers shape these connections, while decision uncertainty, irreversibility, and resolution criteria condition the proposed process. The framework identifies objection–response–commitment traceability as an intermediate process outcome, while distinguishing documented connections from substantive reasoning and realised performance. Its contribution is to specify where critical evaluation may lose organisational influence as AI-generated advice moves towards commitment. For banking leaders, it offers a basis for organising responses to material concerns without assuming that additional review necessarily improves decisions. The framework remains untested and provides an agenda for examining both the benefits and costs of alternative evaluation arrangements.

items.title: StreamCoach: Proactive Sports Coaching via Continuous Visual Reasoning
items.abstract: In fitness and sports training, timely action quality assessment (AQA) is essential for learners to identify and correct technical errors during movement execution. However, most AQA methods assess completed performances, limiting their ability to provide timely feedback. Streaming methods alleviate this latency, but limited reasoning hinders their use of subtle movement cues and sport-specific knowledge. Moreover, their fragmented feedback focuses on one body part at a time, overlooking movement details of other body parts and transitions between action phases. To address these limitations, we propose StreamCoach, a streaming AQA framework under the OnCueCoaching paradigm that couples continuous chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with proactive, evidence-gated coaching. Technique-Aware Reasoning tracks body-part movements and action-phase transitions against sport-specific criteria, while Holistic Coaching integrates accumulated evidence to deliver timely, comprehensive feedback on strengths and technical errors. To support training and benchmarking, we construct EE4D-Stream from 1,213 sports video sequences in Ego-Exo4D through LLM-assisted reannotation and manual review of selected claims, pairing dense CoT annotations with evidence-gated speech content. Building on this dataset, we train StreamCoach using Temporal-Semantic Alignment Reinforcement Learning to jointly optimize feedback timing and content. We benchmark 11 offline and streaming baselines on EE4D-Stream, including three proprietary models. StreamCoach achieves state-of-the-art results across intervention timing, action assessment, and coaching quality, surpassing both GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5.

items.title: Student Perceptions, Trust and Willingness to Use Artificial Intelligence for Career Guidance in Higher Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in career counselling, yet limited questionnaire-based evidence exists on how students perceive and accept it. This study examines students' awareness and experience of AI-based career guidance, its perceived usefulness, trust, ethical and privacy concerns, and willingness to use it. A descriptive, quantitative design was adopted. Data were collected through a structured Google Form from 206 undergraduate and postgraduate students of JG University, Ahmedabad, selected by convenience sampling. All five constructs showed high internal consistency . Prior use of digital or online career-guidance services was reported by of respondents, and had used an AI tool or chatbot for career information. Mean scores for usefulness, trust, ethical concerns, and willingness to use were all above the neutral value of 3 on a five-point scale, mostly between 3.6 and 3.9. Protection of personal information was ranked the most important selection factor. A chi-square test showed a significant but modest association between gender and previous use of digital career-guidance services , with more female than male respondents reporting prior use. Multiple regression showed that perceived usefulness, trust, ethical concerns, and importance of features together explained 75.8% of the variance in willingness to use AI career guidance . Ethical, fairness and privacy concerns were the strongest predictor (β = 0.323), followed by importance of features , trust , and usefulness . The findings suggest that acceptance depends on privacy protection, transparency, and fairness as much as on usefulness. items.title: Students’ Perceptions of AI-Assisted Project-Based Learning for Computational Thinking, Creativity, and Algorithmic Thinking in a Logic and Algorithms Course
items.abstract: Purpose – This study examines students’ self-reported levels and perceptions of computational thinking, creativity, algorithmic thinking, and artificial intelligence (AI) in an AI-assisted project-based learning (PjBL) approach implemented in a Logic and Algorithms course. Design/methodology/approach – A quantitative descriptive approach was employed with 42 first-semester undergraduate students participating in 16 learning sessions during one semester. Students completed individual algorithmic projects with access to generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, according to their learning needs. Data were collected after project completion using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire initially consisting of 20 items, of which 18 items were retained for the final analysis following item-level validity evaluation. Findings – The results showed positive self-reported levels across all four constructs. The mean scores were 3.67 (SD = 0.54) for computational thinking, 3.63 (SD = 0.68) for creativity, 3.68 (SD = 0.52) for algorithmic thinking, and 3.97 (SD = 0.57) for AI perception. All four construct scores were significantly higher than the neutral benchmark of 3.00 (p < .001), with large effect sizes. Research limitations – The study used a one-group posttest design with a relatively small sample from a single Logic and Algorithms course, and the data were based on students’ self-reported perceptions. Therefore, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of causal effects or actual learning gains. Platform preference, fre​quency, and intensity of AI use were not quantitatively analysed. Practical implications: AI-assisted PjBL can provide a flexible environment for exploring and developing solutions to algorithmic problems. Its implementation should be accompanied by lecturer scaffolding, verification and modification of AI-generated outputs, documentation of AI use, and learning activities that encourage original ideas and formal algorithmic representations. Originality/value: This study provides a descriptive account of students’ self-reported computational thinking, creativity, algorithmic thinking, and AI perceptions within an introductory Logic and Algorithms course using AI-assisted PjBL. By examining these dimensions simultaneously, the study highlights the distinction between positive perceptions of AI-supported exploratory problem solving and the need to maintain students’ responsibility for originality, verification, and formal algorithmic reasoning.

items.abstract: This paper highlights the importance and prospects of integrating artificial intelligence technologies into the educational process within the modern education system. It analyzes the potential for using artificial intelligence to automate educational processes, assess student knowledge, analyze learning outcomes, create individualized educational programs, and personalize learning content. The study also examines the role of artificial intelligence in enhancing learning efficiency, reducing routine and repetitive tasks for teachers, identifying individual student needs, and recommending appropriate learning materials. Furthermore, the research addresses ethical, pedagogical, and security issues associated with the use of artificial intelligence, while emphasizing the crucial role of the human factor and direct teacher-student communication in the educational process. The rational and responsible integration of artificial intelligence into education is viewed as a key factor in improving the quality, convenience, and efficiency of education, as well as in preparing students for modern professional life.

items.title: Supervision Consultation as an Organizational Resource to Buffer Occupational Burnout: Proposal of a Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: Background: Occupational burnout is a widespread challenge in contemporary workplaces and is associated with reduced employee well-being, productivity, and organizational sustainability. Although resource-based models emphasize the protective role of personal and job resources, organizational-level interventions targeting burnout remain underexamined. Professional supervision represents a potentially scalable organizational resource that may buffer burnout through the enhancement of personal resources such as occupational self-efficacy, work engagement, and job satisfaction. Objective: The objective of this research proposal is to describe a planned study evaluating whether sustained supervision consultation-delivered face-to-face or online-may buffer occupational burnout indirectly by strengthening key personal resources across diverse occupational groups. Methods: This research proposal describes a planned longitudinal randomized controlled trial with three parallel arms: (1) face-to-face supervision consultation, (2) online supervision consultation, and (3) a waitlist control condition. Structural equation modeling using random-intercept cross-lagged panel models will be used to examine mediation processes over time. Approximately 300 participants from multiple occupational sectors will be recruited. Assessments will be conducted at baseline (T1), 3 months (T2), and 6 months (T3). The proposed intervention consists of 12 biweekly 90-minute group supervision consultation sessions delivered over a 6-month period. Burnout will be measured primarily using the Burnout Assessment Tool (BAT) and supplemented with the Link Burnout Questionnaire (LBQ) to enable comparison across competing conceptualizations. Occupational self-efficacy, work engagement, and job satisfaction will be examined as mediating personal resources. Data will be analyzed using longitudinal structural equation modeling, including mediation and multigroup analyses. Results: As of February 2026, the study protocol has been finalized, but participant recruitment and data collection had not yet commenced. Preparatory work was supported by an internal seed grant awarded in June 2021 under the University of Gdańsk UGrants-first Programme. No data analysis had been conducted. The proposed study remains in the planning stage and will be implemented following ethics approval, trial registration, and acquisition of the necessary resources. Findings from the completed study will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications. Conclusions: This research proposal describes a planned study evaluating supervision consultation as a preventive organizational intervention for burnout. The study aims to contribute to theory-driven, resource-based approaches to occupational well-being and to inform the development of future organizational interventions.

items.title: Supporting, not replacing: counsellors’ and service coordinators’ perspectives on the use of artificial intelligence in youth online chat counselling
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored to support youth online chat counselling services (OCCS). Understanding stakeholders’ perspectives is essential to guide its effective implementation. This study explored counsellors’ and service coordinators’ perspectives on the role of AI in youth online chat counselling. Methods Sixty-two semi-structured interviews were conducted with counsellors and service coordinators from 33 non-profit OCCS across Belgium, Finland, Hungary, and Spain. Interviews were recorded, transcribed verbatim, translated into English, and analysed using qualitative thematic analysis in NVivo. Results Four key themes emerged during interviews: (1) attitudes towards AI, (2) current and (3) future applications, and (4) requirements for responsible implementation. Participants opposed AI replacing human counsellors but considered its growing role as inevitable. 6 out of 33 (18.2%) OCCS reported having incorporated a chatbot (at the time of the interview, type not specified). Participant reported current use of AI in OCCS included automated responses, suicide risk identification, and data management functions. Proposed future uses comprised intelligent routing, multilingual support, transcription, resource and referral identification, counsellor training, real-time suggestions and feedback, and documentation and reporting support. Participants emphasised the need for an AI ethical framework that included transparency and continuous human supervision. Discussion Participants viewed AI as a tool to support rather than replace human counsellors, particularly for administrative and service-delivery tasks. Although concerns remained regarding AI's limitations and potential impact on employment, participants identified opportunities for its use, provided AI is used ethically and responsibly. Future implementation of AI in OCCS should be guided by clear task boundaries, robust ethical safeguards, and the active involvement of counsellors and service coordinators throughout the implementation process.

items.title: The Challenges Facing Young Workers in an Ageing Society — Does AI Really Help
items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence may reshape the effects of population aging on young workers' productivity and human-capital accumulation. Moving beyond the traditional view that aging primarily affects economic growth through labour-supply reductions, the paper considers the possibility that demographic change also weakens cross-age knowledge transmission and workplace learning. Drawing on Mincer's human-capital theory and on an adapted version of Acemoglu and Restrepo's task-based framework, the study conducts a theory-guided qualitative review of existing literature on aging, productivity, AI and young workers. The analysis distinguishes between augmentative AI, which supports workers in completing tasks, and automative AI, which substitutes for tasks previously performed by labour. The literature suggests that augmentative AI may partially offset aging-related productivity losses by transmitting codified expertise and accelerating learning among less-experienced workers. However, automative AI may reduce entry-level employment and learning-by-doing opportunities. The paper concludes that AI's impact on young workers in aging labour markets depends fundamentally on task allocation and its effects on human-capital formation.

items.title: The Effect of Safety Leadership and Work Pressure on Employee Safety Compliance in the Implementation of Occupational Health and Safety (OHS): A Quantitative Study among Construction Field workers in Bogor
items.abstract: Indonesia’s construction industry continues to face a substantial occupational-safety burden, accounting for approximately 31.9% of reported work-accident cases. This study examines whether safety leadership and work pressure are related to safety compliance among field workers at a construction company in Bogor. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was administered to the entire eligible workforce (n = 37), and the data were analysed using multiple linear regression in SPSS. Safety leadership was positively and significantly related to safety compliance, whereas work pressure did not show a significant partial relationship. Considered jointly, the predictors were significant, although they accounted for a modest proportion of variation in compliance (Adjusted R 2 = 16.1%). These results emphasise the value of supervisors’ visible commitment to safety and indicate that additional factors should be investigated when explaining OHS compliance in construction.

items.abstract: This study examines the influence of heuristics within the consumption of second-hand luxury items. Prices on second-hand retail platforms were operationalized to test the anchoring heuristic. A mixed-methods design was employed. The quantitative part involved an online experiment utilizing a simulated second-hand luxury purchase scenario to assess the anchoring effect. The qualitative part consisted of semi-structured expert interviews. The data reveal the influence of the anchoring heuristic being attenuated within the luxury sector but significant and in part contingent upon consumers’ per-purchase internal state. The analysis further suggests that price is not the only critical determinant of consumer choice.

items.title: THE EFFICACY OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ENHANCING WRITING PROFICIENCY AMONG LEARNERS OF CHINESE AS A FOREIGN LANGUAGE
items.abstract: Providing timely, individualized feedback during the writing process remains a persistent Problem of Practice for most language teachers, often leaving learners with delayed support and limited revision opportunities. This mixed-methods crossover study examined whether AI-assisted revision using Claude AI improved Chinese writing performance among high school CFL learners compared with peer revision, whether any advantage transferred to a subsequent unaided writing task, and how learner factors and interactions with AI-generated feedback influenced writing improvement. The study was conducted in a public high school in the eastern United States and involved 40 students in Grades 9–12 enrolled in Chinese 2, Chinese 3, Chinese 4, and AP Chinese courses. Each student completed two five-day writing cycles, revising one essay with AI assistance and one with peer feedback. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, regression, and paired-samples comparisons, while qualitative data from AI interaction logs and survey responses were analyzed using content analysis. Students improved significantly more under AI-assisted revision (M = 1.27 points) than under peer revision (M = 0.13 points; Cohen's d = 1.34), though this advantage did not significantly transfer to a subsequent unaided writing task. Self-rated prompt-writing skill was the only significant predictor of writing improvement. Qualitative findings showed that students most frequently sought AI support for organization, followed by grammar and vocabulary, and perceived AI feedback as helpful while continuing to value teacher feedback. The study highlights prompt literacy as important competency and provides evidence that generative AI can complement, rather than replace, teacher-guided feedback.

items.title: The impact of generative AI application on work efficiency and workload for Generation Z in Jakarta, with AI usage intensity serving as a moderating factor
items.abstract: Despite the fact that generative AI has drastically altered the way Generation Z professionals operate, little research has been done on how it concurrently affects their workload and productivity. We propose that generative AI usage serves as a resource that increases productivity as well as a source of new work demands, and that the intensity of AI usage moderates these impacts. This is based on the Job Demands–Resources theory. We use survey data from 148 Generation Z employees at DKI Jakarta to test our model using PLS-SEM. A productivity paradox is shown by the analysis: the use of generative AI is positively correlated with both work productivity and workload, and the workload impact persists when job demands are the only way to quantify workload. AI usage intensity, the biggest predictor of workload, does not attenuate either connection, suggesting that the demands of generative AI increase with use. By demonstrating that the efficiency gains of generative AI are accompanied by demands that increase with usage, these findings add to the body of research on the adoption of this technology. We talk about the ramifications for businesses looking to use AI without putting too much strain on their employees.

items.title: The New Digital Divide Inside Organizations: AI Access, Career Opportunities and Wage Inequality
items.abstract: Field experiments on generative artificial intelligence (AI) report their largest gains for novices and lower-skilled workers, and this has encouraged a hopeful reading in which the technology narrows skill gaps. Those experiments, however, give access to everybody by design. Inside real organizations, access is allocated by rank, income, occupation and managerial attention. This paper asks who is actually using AI at work, how that use is linked to career opportunities, and what it implies for wage inequality. I combine a structured synthesis of recent experimental, administrative and survey evidence with new calculations on published figures from the Gallup Workforce Panel (more than 30,000 US employees, 2023 to the first quarter of 2026) and Gallup's February 2026 survey of 23,717 employees. Three findings emerge. First, frequent AI use rose in every group, but the gap between leaders and individual contributors grew from 8 to 25 percentage points between 2023 and the second quarter of 2026, even though the ratio between the two stayed near 1.9. Second, frequent use rises by roughly 10 percentage points for each doubling of household income (R² = 0.81 across five income brackets). Third, enabling conditions such as manager support and tool integration are associated with differences of 21 to 34 percentage points in frequent use. A simple break-even calculation shows that the equalizing effect found in experiments disappears once the access ratio between lower- and higher-skilled workers falls to the ratio of their gains per user, and the observed gradients sit close to that threshold under plausible assumptions. Posted wage premiums for AI skills (62 percent on average in 2025) and the fall in early-career hiring in exposed occupations suggest that unequal access can turn into unequal careers. The evidence is descriptive and rests on aggregated secondary data; I set out the limits and a research agenda for linked employer-employee data.

items.title: The Personal PGA Continuity Architecture:
items.abstract: Personal artificial intelligence is often treated as a conversational interface: the user asks, the system answers, and the interaction ends. This white paper proposes a different model. The Personal PGA Continuity Architecture describes a human-centered AI relationship that can adapt not only to the individual, but also to the moment, interface, depth of work, and appropriate return of agency to the human. The framework distinguishes between a mobile or wearable “traveling companion” for immediate capture and clarification and a browser-based deep-work environment for research, analysis, comparison, planning, and document creation. These are presented not as separate intelligences, but as different expressions of one continuing Personal PGA relationship. The paper further explores adaptive depth, pacing, alternative-path exploration, and the Transfer-to-Human Principle (THA), including the idea that returning AI-supported understanding to the human can create space for reflection, reinterpretation, and new human creativity. The central proposition is that meaningful personalization should extend beyond tailored answers to include continuity, modality, pace, depth, alternatives, and preservation of human agency.

items.title: The relationship between LLM usage and critical thinking among college students: the mediating role of task assessment
items.abstract: Objective College students are increasingly using Large Language Models (LLMs) in their studies. This study aims to explore the relationship between LLM usage patterns and college students’ critical thinking and further examine the mediating role of task assessment in this relationship, offering implications for teaching design and policy making. Methods Based on the Expectancy-value theory and the convenience sampling method, a survey was conducted among 544 college students through LLM usage pattern scale, task assessment scale and critical thinking scale. The collected data were interpreted through descriptive statistics, Pearson’s correlation coefficient, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with bootstrap, logistic regression and heterogeneity analysis in Stata. Results Measured on a 5-point Likert scale and computed as the mean of their respective items, Explanatory usage of LLM (EU) was strongly positively associated with task value (VAL, involving intrinsic, attainment, and utility value) (r = 0.735, p < 0.001) and Critical Thinking (CT) (r = 0.694, p < 0.001), while VAL was strongly correlated with CT (r = 0.757, p < 0.001). Generative usage of LLM (GU) was positively correlated with VAL (r = 0.287, p < 0.001) and task cost (COST, including effort, opportunity, and psychological cost) (r = 0.558, p < 0.001). EU highly predicted VAL (β = 0.707, p < 0.001) and CT (β = 0.305, p < 0.001) and Generative Usage of LLM (GU) strongly predicted COST (β = 0.561, p < 0.001). VAL significantly predicted CT (β = 0.565, p < 0.001) and mediated the EU-CT relationship (β = 0.400, p < 0.001), accounting for 56.74% of the total effect. High-EU groups showed higher CT and VAL than low-EU groups (all p < 0.001), and Explorers (high EU, low GU) reported the lowest COST (2.74). Higher VAL reduced the possibility to become Shortcut (low EU, high GU) members by 59.3% (Odd Ratio, OR = 0.407, p < 0.001), while higher COST increased them by 130.7% (OR = 2.307, p < 0.001). Conclusion (1) EU is positively associated with CT both directly and indirectly through higher task value, with the indirect path accounting for 56.74% of the total association. (2) GU shows no significant overall association with CT, but is substantially associated with higher task cost, producing opposite indirect effects through value and cost. (3) High-EU Students show stronger CT, while Explorers report the lowest burden; Low-EU groups perform worse. These findings can help teachers and schools better understand college students’ learning behaviors in the artificial intelligence era, design more valuable learning tasks and enhance students’ critical thinking abilities.

items.title: The Unappreciated Helper: When an AI Facilitation Agent Improves Group Efficiency Despite Poorer User Perceptions
items.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence make it possible to embed AI facilitation agents in collaborative settings, where they can deliver real-time recommendations based on ongoing group discussions. This experimental study examined how group members perceive a collaborative platform with or without such an agent and evaluated the agent’s effects on group communication and performance. A total of 187 undergraduate psychology students collaborated in 50 groups of three or four members on a digital platform with a synchronous text chat. Groups were randomly assigned to one of two conditions (25 groups per condition): with an AI facilitation agent (n = 96 participants) that encouraged information sharing when exchanges were insufficient, or without the agent (n = 91 participants). Participants rated the platform’s acceptability, perceived support, sense of intrusion, and affective reactions. Participants in the AI condition rated the platform as less acceptable and less supportive, but not more intrusive or unpleasant. Nevertheless, groups assisted by the agent were more efficient, completing the task faster with less communicative effort. Descriptive analyses of group interactions in the three minutes before and after the agent’s interventions showed a shift from providing information toward requesting information, expressing opinions, and agreeing, without change in overall interaction volume. These findings reveal a gap between objective performance and subjective perceptions, highlighting the need to design AI agents that improve group efficiency while fostering members’ sense of support and acceptance.

items.title: THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS IN ENGLISH LANGUAGE LEARNING: COMMON PROBLEMS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR EFFECTIVE PRACTICE
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as chatbots, translation applications, grammar checkers, and speech-recognition programs have rapidly entered the everyday lives of students and teachers. Many learners now use them to prepare for lessons, write texts, and practise speaking. However, the results of such use are not always positive. Students frequently use AI tools in ways that bring quick answers but little real learning, and teachers are often unsure how to guide this process. This article examines the most common problems that arise when students use AI tools to develop Reading, Writing, Listening, and Speaking skills. It also discusses the role of psychological and ethical factors and offers practical recommendations that can help teachers and learners use AI as a support for learning rather than a substitute for it.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, particularly large language models (LLMs), are increasingly used by clinicians and medical learners despite growing concerns about negative impacts on core elements of physician development including knowledge acquisition, skill proficiency, and professional identity formation. In this position paper, we describe the risks and benefits of AI integration, a taxonomy of tasks (AI-only, human and AI, and human-only), and specific scenarios for each type of task. We provide recommendations on behalf of the Society of General Internal Medicine on how medical educators and institutions can thoughtfully integrate AI into training, emphasizing how to prepare learners to leverage these technologies to augment rather than replace their clinical performance.

items.title: Transforming English Teaching Strategies With Intelligent Voice Technology: Pathways for Web-Enhanced Classrooms
items.abstract: This study proposes a tiered progression with a closed-loop feedback model to optimize English teaching in web-enhanced classrooms through collaboration between humans and artificial intelligence, supported by data-driven intervention. By comparing traditional and innovative strategies in 10 classes (n = 200) over 18 weeks using platform logs, observations, surveys, and interviews, the study constructs an input–process–result variable system. Results show that teachers' average response time was 22.0 s, grouping interaction frequency increased from 3.1 to 6.4 times/week, and oral English scores improved by an average of 11.5 points under the innovation strategy versus 5.2 points under the traditional strategy. Intervention frequency was positively correlated with oral performance (r = 0.48, p < 0.01) and, together with the artificial intelligence score, was significantly positively associated with it (p < 0.01). Challenges include teachers' differing technical adaptability and delayed responses from low-participation students. This study provides preliminary evidence and a framework for optimizing web-based language education.

items.title: Trustworthy and Explainable AI for Electric Vehicle Reliability: A Four-Domain Analysis of Powertrain Systems and Intelligent Driving Experiences
items.abstract: As electrified powertrains and advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) develop rapidly, consumer assessments of new energy vehicles (NEVs) increasingly encompass powertrain performance, intelligent driving functionality, and operational safety rather than conventional driving attributes alone. Overall star ratings cannot adequately distinguish users' experience of battery range and charging reliability from their assessments of environmental perception, driving decisions, and human takeover. This study proposes a four-dimensional framework for analysing NEV owner reviews and integrates topic modelling, sentiment identification, structured rating cues, and community endorsement into an analytical design. The four domains comprise battery range and energy efficiency (T0), charging replenishment and electric-drive reliability (T1), driving-environment perception and scenario adaptation (T2), and driving decision-making and safety takeover (T3). The supplied analytical dataset comprises 16,500 records associated with the BYD Tang New Energy and AITO M9 vehicle labels. The reported results show that T0 accounts for 29.10% of dominant-topic records, whereas T3 displays the highest mean endorsement count (8.753). Negative binomial regression suggests heterogeneous conditional associations between technical themes and observable endorsement, with a positive T3-by-rating-extremity interaction (β = 0.408). These descriptive and model-based patterns illustrate the importance of analytically separating topical prevalence, affective evaluations, and platform interactions. The study contributes a vehicle-specific construct system, an integrated natural language processing and count-regression workflow, and a foundation for interpreting technology-specific user feedback. These findings must be interpreted in light of the underlying data provenance and the distinction between perceived experience and objectively verified technical safety.

items.title: Understanding burnout and resilience among healthcare professionals in Canada
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Burnout among healthcare professionals has emerged as one of the most pressing occupational health crises of the 21st century. Resilience is an individual trait known to protect against burnout, yet the connection between resilience and burnout among healthcare professionals remains unclear. AIMS: This study aimed to assess the relationship between burnout and resilience among healthcare professionals. METHODS: A cross-sectional, descriptive-correlational survey design was used. The theoretical framework combined Maslach's Burnout Framework and Resiliency Theory to situate findings within both psychosocial and organizational contexts. RESULTS: Burnout scores for the sample indicated that the average healthcare worker in Ontario was experiencing moderate emotional exhaustion (Mean of 19 out of 54), high depersonalization (Mean of 15 out of 30) and moderate to high personal accomplishment (Mean of 35 out of 48). Resilience rates for the sample suggested that the average Ontarian healthcare worker possessed a moderate/normal level of resilience (Mean of 3 out of 5, reflecting an adequate ability to recover following stress/adversity). Higher burnout (emotional exhaustion and depersonalization) was observed among more experienced workers and among frontline workers. Gender had no significant influence. Resilience showed limited correlation with burnout. CONCLUSIONS: Burnout was widespread among healthcare professionals, suggesting that individual coping capacity alone may be insufficient to mitigate the cumulative effects of occupational stress.

items.title: Understanding the Learning Journey: How Drivers Learn to Use In-Vehicle Systems
items.abstract: As in-vehicle systems become increasingly complex, understanding how drivers learn to use them is critical for safety, usability, and adoption. This qualitative study explores how drivers learn to use in-vehicle systems—media, navigation, and ADAS—through semi-structured interviews with sixteen participants in their own stationary vehicles. Using a general inductive approach, six themes were identified: Learning methods and sources; Familiarity, trust and mental models; Interface design and usability; User engagement and autonomy; System behavior and limitations; Safety and driving context. Based on these findings, we propose a preliminary framework that conceptualizes learning demands through understanding the learning characteristics of drivers. This framework, the Learning Exclusion Model for In-Vehicle Systems, extends capability–demand frameworks to conceptualize learning exclusion as a mismatch between system learning demands and driver characteristics within specific contexts. Results highlight a gap between the availability of systems and drivers’ ability to learn them, emphasizing the need for more inclusive in-vehicle systems.

items.title: Unifying Partner and Environment Diversity to Improve Human-AI Coordination
items.abstract: Real-world applications of modern AI systems require generalization to both unseen environments and novel human users. The field of zero-shot coordination (ZSC) has focused primarily on deploying AI to cooperate with novel partners in otherwise familiar environments. Popular population-based methods achieve this by partnering the agent with a diversity of simulated human users during training in a fixed environment, but does not consider the more realistic scenario where both the users and the environment are unseen during training. Recently, training across environments has been explored in training a single self-play agent, which shows better generalization on both novel human users and unseen environments. In this work, we ask whether jointly modeling partner diversity and environment diversity yields stronger coordination with novel partners in novel environments. We introduce Cross Environment Co-Play (CECP), a two-stage framework that first trains a population of self-play agents across a distribution of procedurally generated environments, and then trains a cooperator policy against this partner population. To further couple social and environmental reasoning, we add a next-state prediction module that encourages representations to encode both partner behavior and task structure. We evaluate CECP on both a neuroscience-inspired cooperative foraging task, and the popular ZSC benchmark Overcooked, under held-out partner and held-out environment conditions. CECP achieves the strongest performance among the compared baselines and attains state-of-the-art results under our evaluation protocol for human-AI collaboration. We analyze the model's latent representation encoded by the next-state prediction module, showing it can not only improve the performance of the cooperative AI, but also provide more interpretable latents, demonstrated by the inference of partner skill levels.

items.title: Unpacking interpretability: Human-centered criteria for optimal combinatorial solutions
items.abstract: Algorithmic support systems can return solutions that are optimal but hard to interpret for humans. A given problem can have multiple, equally optimal solutions that differ substantially in how interpretable they are. Yet there is no precise account of what makes one solution more interpretable than another. To identify structural properties associated with interpretability, we studied a packing paradigm based on the multiple subset sum problem (MSSP), in which participants judged which of two equally optimal solutions for packing items into bins was easier to understand. We found that preferences reliably tracked three properties of solution structure: alignment with a greedy heuristic, simple within-bin composition, and how ordered the visual representation was. The strongest associations were observed for ordered representations and alignment with a greedy heuristic. Compositional simplicity also showed a consistent association. Reaction-time evidence was mixed; the only reliable result was faster responses when heuristic differences were larger. Webcam-based results of aggregate gaze times did not show reliable associations with the three solution properties. In summary, these results ground interpretability (at least in our packing paradigm) in measurable structural properties of solutions. By identifying these properties (simple compositions, ordered representation, and alignment with a heuristic) our findings motivate interpretability-aware optimization and presentation of machine solutions. They also outline a path to quantify trade-offs between optimality and interpretability in allocation and design tasks.

items.title: User experience of a custom augmented reality-based exergame for children with cerebral palsy and acquired brain injuries
items.abstract: Conventional pediatric rehabilitation for cerebral palsy (CP) or acquired brain injury (ABI) prioritizes motor outcomes, often neglecting cognitive deficits and their interplay. Sessions are often perceived as repetitive and demotivating, reducing engagement. Immersive exergaming, especially through augmented reality (AR), enables simultaneous cognitive-motor training in safe, interactive settings. There is little evidence on immersive exergames for these children, and no immersive AR exergames target cognitive-motor rehabilitation or report on user experience (UX). This study aims to assess the overall UX of a purpose-built immersive AR exergame for children with brain injuries. Twenty-nine children (11.8 ± 1.6 years; 12 CP/17 ABI) participated in two sessions using the Microsoft HoloLens2, each involving one cognitive-motor AR game (AR Corsi and AR Zoo). UX was assessed through standardized questionnaires: System Usability Scale (usability), Technology Acceptance Model (acceptance), AttrakDiff (perceived experience quality), MeCue (emotions), Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (motivation), and Rating scale of Perceived Exertion for Children (fatigue). The exergame was well accepted and perceived as easy to use. Scores for motivation, emotions, and perceived experience quality were high and positive. A small but significant increase in mental and physical fatigue was observed after the sessions (P < .01). No significant differences were found between the two game conditions. This immersive AR exergame demonstrates a positive UX in children with brain injuries, supporting its potential use in rehabilitation. These results emphasize the importance of conducting comprehensive UX assessments when developing innovative rehabilitation tools and provide a basis for future investigations into therapeutic impact.

items.title: Validating Multi-Model AI-Generated Acceptance Criteria in Requirements Engineering
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering to generate artifacts such as requirements, user stories, acceptance criteria, documentation, and code. Their use in requirements engineering raises important questions about correctness, traceability, and hallucination, especially because flawed specifications can affect later design, implementation, and verification activities. While much recent work on AI-assisted software engineering has focused on code generation and code-level validation, the validation of AI-generated specifications has received less attention. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a validation-oriented approach for AI-generated acceptance criteria. The approach combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), multi-model generation, and an explicitly structured human-in-the-loop workflow. We describe a working prototype that allows users to prepare or enter user stories, generate acceptance criteria using several LLMs, optionally augment generation with retrieved requirements-related examples, compare outputs side by side, inspect retrieved context, and select, edit, or regenerate candidate criteria before explicitly submitting a reviewer-finalized version. The system also records model outputs, user interventions, retrieval settings, and final criteria as part of a logged decision process. Rather than claiming that generation accuracy is already improved, the contribution of this work is to operationalize validation as an explicit, inspectable, and accountable process for AI-generated requirements artifacts.

items.title: Vivir y crear en la era de la inteligencia artificial: trayectoria personal encarnada y reflexiones
items.abstract: The essay reflects on creation and living in the era of Artificial Intelligence, marked by “dromology,” or a speed that prevents the calm necessary for thinking and building. The author explores her evolution toward Vital Motricity, a paradigm in which corporeality and action are the central axes of consciousness and planetary ethics. Although she uses AI as a tool for synthesis, she warns that it lacks consciousness, empathy, and genuine creative capacity, functioning only as a data processor. She denounces the alienating power of big tech companies and the risks of social exclusion they entail. Finally, she proposes a reflective form of resistance through the act of questioning and embodied walking, urging the recovery of human agency in the face of the convenience of screens.

items.title: When Manufactured Watermarking Misleads Thought: AI Provenance, Human Source Erasure, and the Asymmetry of Attribution
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence watermarking and digital provenance mechanisms increasingly address whether an output was generated or modified by an artificial system. Although such identification can support transparency and accountability, it does not necessarily establish the intellectual origin of the knowledge, reasoning, methods, or creative contributions represented in the resulting material. This publication introduces Manufactured Watermarking as a conceptual condition in which AI-output identification may be treated as a complete account of intellectual provenance, leaving identifiable earlier human contributions insufficiently recognised. The research distinguishes technological production from intellectual origination and examines Source–Benefit Asymmetry, Source-to-Suspect Reversal, and the risks of treating technical uncertainty as evidence against human authorship. Four exploratory case studies examine AI-content detection, AI-assisted conceptual development, website-template generation, and AI-assisted artistic creation. These cases illustrate questions of Source recognition, attribution, creative continuity, and the limits of output-level identification. They are qualitative exploratory investigations, not controlled demonstrations of systemic infringement or proven misconduct. The publication proposes Human-Origin Watermarking as a conceptual research direction for preserving evidence of identifiable human intellectual formation, Human–AI contributions, chronological continuity, and relationships between originating Sources and subsequent developments. It also considers Legacy Watermarking as a means of recognising earlier human and historical contributions across technological transformations. The central argument is that identifying an artificial producer and preserving an originating human intellectual contribution are distinct requirements of provenance. Neither establishes the other. Publication contents Part 1 - Main Manuscript: The authored conceptual research, definitions, analytical distinctions, limitations, and proposed research direction. Part 2 - Case Studies Dossier: Four exploratory investigations, supporting observations, documentation, figures, and references. Part 3 - Visual Introduction: An accessible visual explanation of the research for readers unfamiliar with AI provenance and Human-AI cognition. It is intendent for introductory understanding and quich reference. It does not replace or supersede the Main Manuscript or Case Studies Dossier. Part 4 - Claude HTML Research Site Template: An AI-generated website-template artifact examined in Case Study 3, preserved as an accompanying research exhibit rather than a functioning research platform. items.title: Who Attributes a Mind to Whom? Mutual Theory of Mind in Simulated User-Assistant Conversation
items.abstract: When users assume that an AI chatbot has mental states, they are more likely to develop over-reliance, emotional dependence, and in extreme cases, psychological harm or self-harm. However, how these mind attributions arise in conversations and how human or AI factors influence this is still unknown. We study how users attribute minds using a minimal framework: a simulated user with different characteristics chats with assistants that differ in social style and memory. We also introduce a message-level measure of who attributes a mind to whom in four directions, checked with trained coders and applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge. Our results show that, on average, nine out of thirteen characteristics raised simulated users' attribution to the assistant. We found that relational needs such as attachment anxiety raised it as theory predicts, some general personality traits raised it as well, and AI-specific characteristics the least. By contrast, the assistant's social style barely changed simulated users' mind attribution. Instead, sycophantic instructions raised the assistant's attribution to itself. Memory raised users' attribution only with some user models. The model playing the user changed overall attribution and the effects of characteristics, style, and memory. Our framework measures how persona descriptions affect mind attribution in simulation. It gives concrete hypotheses for human studies and shows the need for more consistent user simulators.
